parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Good morning, everyone. In today’s psychology lecture, I’ll be talking about human memory and what I want to do first is establish the historical context. So I’ll outline various ideas about human memory and how they’ve changed over time.

So first, early cultures. Now, in the earliest times, let’s say before 3000 years BC, people were dependent on being able to remember things, perhaps even more than we are today. That’s because humans could not write, the skill hadn’t been developed. So a good memory was important. For one thing, it helped people navigate in the area around their homes, and it was the only way to access family history and ancestry. Once more, a good memory might be the difference between life and death. Most people were hunters and gatherers, so it was essential to understand which foods were poisonous and which were not. This was particularly true of plants because they sometimes looked very similar; and the only way to store this information and pass it on to the next generation was to remember it. Unfortunately, because it was so long ago, there’s limited information about what techniques we used to assist memory.

Okay, so moving on now to the ancient Greeks, and the Greek poet named Simonides, who lived around 500 BC, was the man sometimes described as the father of memory training. Simonides’ most important idea was that it’s much easier to remember information if we connect it with one particular place. Then, over hundreds of years, other Greek scholars developed his ideas about memory, and a lot of this information has survived. So we know that, by the first century, the Greeks believed that people could use their human senses to improve their memory, and this was particularly true when it came to sight. There was a strong connection there they believed.

Well, next I should talk about the ancient Romans, who, like the Greeks, believed memory training was extremely important. They used memory in many different ways, obviously, but most of all, in ancient Rome, people thought that one of the greatest skills was the ability to give an impressive speech in public, and memory was one of the keys to doing that. So this was why, from about 100 BC, the Romans wanted to develop techniques to improve memory. And an important figure here was Cicero, a Roman political leader. One of Cicero’s ideas was that humans actually have two types of memory: There’s a memory that can be developed, which he called the artificial memory, and there’s another type of memory which he called natural. And the point is that you can learn techniques to help improve your artificial memory, an idea that’s interested some academics ever since.

So, moving next to later European history, and the first thing to note is that, during the Middle Ages, a group of academics called the Scholastics were also interested in memory techniques. The Scholastics used these techniques when they were instructing pupils about religion, and this raised the profile of memory techniques. But later, attitudes towards memory began to change, and this started in the 17th century. People began to see memory training as an art form, and that didn’t interest them so much anymore, because they thought that science had the answers to most human questions. This attitude really continued into the 19th century as well. Children weren’t taught memory techniques, but were expected to learn lots of facts, and to do this by constantly repeating things like dates and so on.

Okay, so then we come to modern times, and in the 1940s a remarkable series of studies was conducted with a man known simply as S. Psychologists found that S never made notes about anything, although he was a journalist and never forgot facts. The researchers concluded that S had an unusual medical condition, which meant he developed incredible memory skills. This was important as it seemed to support the ideas of the ancient Greeks and other much earlier scholars, but in the late part of the 20th century, the focus switched to computers.

Okay, well that’s the historical context.

analyses.content: 录音中提到因为人类 could not write（不会写字），这项技能还没开发出来，所以只能依赖记忆。
That’s because humans could not write, the skill hadn’t been developed.
题目中的 "unable to" 对应录音中的 "could not"，直接填后面的动词原形。
Most people were hunters and gatherers, so it was essential to understand which foods were poisonous... This was particularly true of plants because they sometimes looked very similar.
题目是 "such as some types of..."（例如某种...），这是举例信号，不要填 broad category 词汇如 "foods"。
演讲者说分辨有毒食物对 plants（植物）来说尤其如此，因为它们长得很像。
Simonides’ most important idea was that it’s much easier to remember information if we connect it with one particular place.
题目中的 "linked to" 对应录音中的 "connect it with"，听到连接词后紧跟的名词就是答案。
Simonides 认为如果我们将信息与一个特定的 place（地点）联系起来，就更容易记住。
So we know that, by the first century, the Greeks believed that people could use their human senses to improve their memory, and this was particularly true when it came to sight.
题目中的 "especially" 对应录音中的 "particularly true"，不要填 senses，那是统称。
古希腊人认为感官能帮助记忆，对于 sight（视觉）来说尤其如此。
...people thought that one of the greatest skills was the ability to give an impressive speech in public, and memory was one of the keys to doing that.
题目中的 "Making a good..." 对应录音中的 "give an impressive..."，核心名词是 speech。
在古罗马，人们认为最重要的技能之一就是能在公共场合发表令人印象深刻的 speech（演讲）。
Cicero 认为人类有两种记忆：一种是可以开发的（人工的），另一种是他所称的 natural（天生的/自然的）记忆。
There’s a memory that can be developed, which he called the artificial memory, and there’s another type of memory which he called natural.
题目说 "in addition to..."（除了...之外），说明要填除了 "can be developed" 之外的另一种，即 natural，不要填 artificial。
The Scholastics used these techniques when they were instructing pupils about religion, and this raised the profile of memory techniques.
题目中的 "teach" 对应录音中的 "instructing pupils about"，后面紧跟的宾语就是答案。
经院哲学家（Scholastics）在教学生关于 religion（宗教）的知识时使用了这些记忆技巧。
People began to see memory training as an art form, and that didn’t interest them so much anymore, because they thought that science had the answers to most human questions.
题目中的 "provide explanations" 对应录音中的 "had the answers"，那个主语就是 science。
到了17世纪，人们不再对记忆训练感兴趣，因为他们认为 science（科学）已经有了大多数问题的答案。
Children weren’t taught memory techniques, but were expected to learn lots of facts, and to do this by constantly repeating things like dates and so on.
题目中的 "such as" 对应录音中的 "things like"，这是雅思听力最经典的举例考点。
19世纪的学生被要求通过不断重复来学习事实，比如 dates（日期）之类的东西。
Psychologists found that S never made notes about anything, although he was a journalist and never forgot facts.
注意拼写 journalist，不要听到 psychologists 就填，那是做研究的人。
研究对象 'S' 虽然是一名 journalist（记者），但他从不做笔记却能记住事实。
